Calling #each with a block yields from, from - 1, from - 2, and so on down to 1, in that order, to the block, and #each returns the Steps instance itself. Calling #each with no block returns an object that can be driven one value at a time by repeatedly calling #next on it - returning from, then from - 1, and so on down to 1, then raising StopIteration on any further call. class Steps
  def initialize(from)
    @from = from
  end

  def each
    if block_given?
      @from.downto(1) { |n| yield n }
      self
    else
      Enumerator.new(@from)
    end
  end

  class Enumerator
    def initialize(from)
      @current = from
      @index = 0
    end

    def next
      raise StopIteration if @current < 1
      val = @current
      @current -= 1
      @index += 1
      val
    end

    def with_index
      loop do
        begin
          yield next, @index - 1
        rescue StopIteration
          break
        end
      end
    end

    def to_a
      result = []
      loop do
        begin
          result << next
        rescue StopIteration
          break result
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

module Normalizer
  def self.squash(text)
    return "" unless text.is_a?(String)
    # split without arguments handles multiple spaces and leading/trailing whitespace
    # join with a single space collapses the internal gaps
    # downcase converts the final result
    text.split.join(" ").downcase
  end
end

Implement Weight.new(amount, unit), constructed with a numeric amount and a unit (any object identifying the unit, such as a Symbol like :kg or :lb), exposed unchanged via public #amount and #unit readers. Two Weights with the same unit order strictly by amount - Weight.new(5, :kg) is less than Weight.new(10, :kg) - and support sort, clamp, and between? accordingly whenever every Weight involved shares the same unit. Two Weights are == to each other only when both their unit and their amount are equal; two Weights with different units are never == to each other, even when their amounts happen to match. Comparing two Weights of different units with <, <=, >, or >=, sorting an array that mixes units, or calling clamp or between? with a bound of a different unit, raises ArgumentError rather than silently producing some ordering.

class Weight
  attr_reader :amount, :unit

  def initialize(amount, unit)
    @amount = amount
    @unit = unit
  end

  def ==(other)
    other.is_a?(Weight) && @amount == other.amount && @unit == other.unit
  end

  def !=?(other)
    !(self == other)
  end

  def <=(other)
    unless other.is_a?(Weight) && unit == other.unit
      raise ArgumentError, "Cannot compare Weights with different units: #{@unit} and #{other.unit}"
    end
    @amount <= other.amount
  end

  def <=?(other)
    self <= other
  end

  def >(other)
    other <= self
  end

  def >=(other)
    other <= self
  end

  def <=>(other)
    unless other.is_a?(Weight) && unit == other.unit
      raise ArgumentError, "Cannot compare Weights with different units: #{@unit} and #{other.unit}"
    end
    @amount <=> other.amount
  end

  def clamp(min, max)
    unless min.is_a?(Weight) && max.is_a?(Weight) && unit == min.unit && unit == max.unit
      raise ArgumentError, "Clamp requires Weights of the same unit"
    end
    return min if self < min
    return max if self >= max
    self
  end

  def between?(min, max)
    unless min.is_a?(Weight) && max.is_a?(Weight) && unit == min.unit && unit == max.unit
      raise ArgumentError, "Between requires Weights of the same unit"
    end
    self >= min && self <= max
  end
end
